Effectively exhausted for personal property (recovery 20 years or less) but a calculator holding such an asset should apply it (my reasoning, not an agency statement). NOL: 143.121.2(4) limits Missouri NOL deductions to a 20-year carryforward and 2-year carryback, with exceptions for 172(b)(1)(G) and 172(i); a loss created by bonus or 179 is therefore tracked separately from the federal NOL (my reading of the statute; Form MO-5090 is the DOR's NOL addition sheet, not read). 163(j): 143.121.2(6) and 3(11) (tax years from 2018) let Missouri subtract interest disallowed under 163(j) in the year disallowed and add it back in the year later deducted federally.

2023.summary: Income Tax Notice 80-23-003 (20 Oct 2023), HB 1733 (signed 27 Mar 2023, effective 1 Jan 2023): for tax years beginning after 31 Dec 2022, expenditures for qualified property or qualified improvement property are eligible for 100% bonus depreciation and may be deducted in the year placed in service. 'Qualified property' means 168(k) and 'qualified improvement property' means 168(e)(6), each as they existed on 1 Jan 2021. The taxpayer may elect the bonus 'and/or' depreciate under IRC 168; the election is by the return due date including extensions and is irrevocable unless the Commissioner allows a change. The total of all methods cannot exceed 100% of cost. The rate is a state rate, independent of the federal phase-down (federal was 80% for 2023).

2021.summary: NC decouples from 168(k) and 168(n) bonus. 2021 D-401 Schedule S line 3: 'North Carolina did not adopt the 100% bonus depreciation provisions in IRC sections 168(k) or 168(n) for property placed in service for tax year 2021. You must add 85% of the amount of bonus depreciation deducted on your federal return to your state return.' Then 'you may deduct 20% of the amount added back in the first five taxable years beginning with tax year 2022' (Schedule S line 22 for 2016-2020 add-backs, lines 22f/23f). Net: 15% of the federal bonus is effectively allowed in year 1; the other 85% comes back in five equal 17% (= 20% x 85%) slices over 2022-2026. Regular MACRS on the whole basis continues; the add-back is an AGI adjustment on Schedule S, not a separate depreciation schedule.
2021.source_citation: NCDOR 2021 Form D-401 instruction booklet, Instructions for D-400 Schedule S (p.17 IRC date, lines 3, 4; p.19 lines 21-23); G.S. 105-153.6 as cited there; https://www.ncdor.gov/taxes-forms/individual-income-tax/filing-topics/adjustment-bonus-depreciation

Bonus asset basis (line 21, G.S. 105-153.6(e),(f)): on an actual or deemed transfer after 1 Jan 2013 with carryover federal basis, the transferee adds any remaining bonus deductions allowed to the asset's basis and depreciates the adjusted basis over the remaining life; the transferor gets no future deductions. Line 6/27 handle federal-vs-state basis differences on property disposed of. IRC reference as of 1 Apr 2021 (not tracking later federal changes). NC rate 5.25%. 2021.summary: ND individual tax starts from federal taxable income: N.D.C.C. 57-38-30.3(2) defines North Dakota taxable income as 'the federal taxable income of an individual, estate, or trust as computed under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended, adjusted as follows' (subdivisions a-t: US interest, capital-gain/dividend exclusion, lump-sum, military pay, etc.). No subdivision adjusts depreciation, 168(k), 168(n) or 179, and 57-38-30.3(1) limits a taxpayer to 'those adjustments or credits that are specifically provided for in this section'. The 2021 Schedule ND-1SA (read) lists only renaissance zone, new or expanding business, organ donor, workforce recruitment, stillborn child, National Guard/Reserve pay and college reimbursement subtractions - no depreciation line. So federal bonus (100% for 2021) and 179 flow through.

2021.special_rules: No state depreciation schedule: use the federal Form 4562 and Schedule C/E/F figures. ND starts from federal TAXABLE income (after the federal standard/itemized deduction), so there is no separate ND deduction add-back for depreciation. Sole proprietors may claim the new or expanding business income exemption (N.D.C.C. ch. 40-57.1; ND-1SA line for 2021: line 2) and renaissance zone exemption (line 1) against business income. A filer with no federal return computes a pro forma federal taxable income first (57-38-30.3(1)). N.D.C.C. 57-38-01(5)(a)-(c) retain 1983-1989 ACRS and section 168(f)(8) leasing nonadoption rules that matter only to pre-1990 property.

2021.summary: Gross Income Tax (GIT) depreciation is computed without the federal special depreciation allowance. N.J.S.A. 54A:5-1.2 (P.L. 2004, c.65) decouples assets placed in service on or after 1 Jan 2004. GIT-DEP (Revised 8/19): 'The federal 50% Special Depreciation Allowance is not allowed', and only a 30% allowance 'is allowed only if it was taken for federal tax purposes'. NJ basis = federal basis before special allowance/179/depreciation, less the NJ 179 deduction; NJ depreciation uses the federal method and life. The adjustment (federal depreciation incl. bonus and 179, minus NJ 179, minus NJ depreciation) goes on GIT-DEP line 7 each year until the asset is fully depreciated or disposed of. The forms name only the 30% and 50% rates; they do not mention the 100% (2021) bonus, so 'none' for that rate is the Division's rule applied by inference.

2021.special_rules: Max NJ 179 is 25,000 total per income category (net profits from business; rents/royalties) per individual, partnership or S corporation; the federal reduced-dollar limitation applies using 25,000 as the maximum; no business-income limit; unused 179 and unused adjustment cannot be carried forward or back or used against another category. One GIT-DEP per category (e.g., all rental properties on one worksheet). Adjusts 179 recapture income and gain/loss on disposition. If the first NJ adjustment was never reported (error not corrected by the Division, or no NJ filing requirement), NJ basis equals federal basis and no adjustment is required or allowed later. Liberty Zone property: 179 max 60,000. Partnerships and S corporations with an NJ filing requirement compute their own adjustment (NJ-1065 line 13c/15f; CBT-100S Sch K).

2021.summary: New Mexico personal income tax starts from federal adjusted gross income (TRD: 'Personal income tax in New Mexico starts with the Federally Adjusted Gross Income (FAGI) from your federal return'). The 2021 PIT-ADJ lists the only permitted additions (lines 1-4: tax-exempt bond interest, federal NOL carryover, 529 refunds, conservation-land charitable deduction) and says 'If an item is not listed, it is not a valid New Mexico addition, exemption, or deduction for this schedule.' There is no depreciation or 168(k) line, so the federal bonus deduction flows through Schedule C/E/F into FAGI unchanged.
2021.source_citation: NM TRD, 2021 PIT-ADJ Instructions (General Information; lines 1-4 additions; no depreciation line); TRD Personal Income Tax Overview https://www.tax.newmexico.gov/individuals/personal-income-tax-information-overview/; NMSA 7-2-2 ('adjusted gross income' = IRC 62 'as that section may be amended or renumbered')

2021.special_rules: No NM basis difference arises for a sole proprietor or rental owner, so one depreciation schedule serves federal and NM. A NM NOL is limited to a federal NOL, no carryback, 19-year carryforward for losses incurred on or after 1 Jan 2013 (PIT-ADJ line 7). 2021.summary: NY does not allow the federal 168(k) special depreciation for property placed in service on or after 1 Jun 2003 (tax years beginning after 31 Dec 2002). Add back ALL federal depreciation deducted on 168(k) property (IT-225 addition A-209, from IT-398 col G) and subtract NY depreciation computed 'under IRC section 167, as that section would have applied to the property if it had been acquired on September 10, 2001' i.e. ordinary MACRS with no special allowance (IT-225 subtraction S-213, IT-398 col F). Year of disposition: S-214 = total federal depreciation minus total NY depreciation on that property. Exceptions: qualified resurgence zone property and NY Liberty Zone property (IRC 1400L(b)(2)). Read on the 2025 IT-398 and the 2022-2024 IT-225-I; the 2021 forms were not read.
2021.source_citation: NY Tax Law 607(a) (nysenate.gov); Tax Law 612(b)(8), (c)(16) as cited in IT-398 instructions; NY TAX 'New York State tax implications of federal COVID relief for tax years beginning before January 1, 2022' https://www.tax.ny.gov/pit/cares-act-faq.htm; 2025 IT-398 https://www.tax.ny.gov/pdf/current_forms/it/it398_fill_in.pdf
2021.verify_note: Statute and FAQ read via the fetch summariser (607(a) text returned verbatim and confirmed on a second fetch). The 2021 IT-225-I / IT-398 were not read; the 168(k) rule is taken from the 2025 IT-398 ('For tax years beginning after December 31, 2002') and the 2022-2024 IT-225-I. 179 conformity is inferred from the absence of any 179 modification in the instructions read, not from a sentence.
2021.change_note: For taxable years beginning before 1 Jan 2022 Tax Law 607(a) provides that 'any amendments made to the internal revenue code of nineteen hundred eighty-six after March first, two thousand twenty shall not apply to this article'.
2021.special_rules: Qualified improvement property (QIP): NY personal income tax does NOT conform to the CARES Act QIP changes (15-year MACRS, 20-year ADS) for tax years before 2022 (TAX FAQ 'New York State tax implications of federal COVID relief for tax years beginning before January 1, 2022'); QIP therefore keeps its pre-CARES class life (39-year) for NY, differences reported on IT-558 for 2020-2021 per the FAQ. 179: no NY modification found, so the federal 179 limit applies (the 1,050,000 / 2,620,000 figure is the Rev. Proc. 2020-45 inflation adjustment, not a post-3/1/2020 amendment). The A-209/S-213 adjustments are made on the full amounts even if passive-activity limits cut the federal deduction (Tax Law 612(b)(8), (c)(16), per IT-398). Resident and part-year/nonresident filers complete IT-398 as a full-year resident.

2025.summary: 2025 IT-398 (read in full): 'For tax years beginning after December 31, 2002, NYS does not allow the federal special depreciation deduction for IRC § 168(k) property ... placed in service inside or outside NYS after May 31, 2003. Instead, you are allowed a NYS depreciation deduction determined under IRC § 167, as that section would have applied to the property if it had been acquired on September 10, 2001.' Addition A-209 = federal depreciation deducted on the property (IT-398 col G); subtraction S-213 = NY depreciation (col F), computed with the convention from federal Form 4562 col E and any consistent method allowed 'without regard to § 168(k)'; basis is reduced by any 179 expensing; disposition S-214. So the new 100% bonus for property acquired after 19 Jan 2025 (and the 40% on earlier-acquired property) is disallowed. Layer check: Rev. Proc. 2024-40 (40%; 179 at 1,250,000 / 3,130,000) is superseded by P.L. 119-21, but NY disregards bonus either way; for 179 NY has no figure of its own.

2021.summary: Ohio decouples from 168(k) and 179 expensing by an add-back and a five-year give-back. R.C. 5747.01(A)(17) (current text via FindLaw, 'current as of January 01, 2026'): add 5/6 of the depreciation allowed by IRC 168(k), plus 5/6 of qualifying 179 expense; (A)(18): deduct one-fifth of the amount so added in each of the five succeeding taxable years. Substitutions: for taxable years beginning in 2012 or later, 2/3 replaces 5/6 (and 1/2 over two years is deducted) if the taxpayer's Ohio income tax withheld rose 10% or more over the prior year, and no add-back if the withholding increase equals or exceeds the depreciation; 'the entire' amount (6/6, deducted 1/6 over six years) replaces 5/6 if a net operating loss results from the depreciation. Default result: year 1 deduction keeps 1/6 (16.67%) of the federal 168(k) amount, the other 5/6 returns at 1/6 (= 1/5 x 5/6) of the add-back per year for five years. The agency FAQ (search excerpt, tax.ohio.gov Income - Bonus Depreciation): the amount subject to add-back is 'total 179 expense less $25,000 plus all 168(k) depreciation expense'. Reported on the Ohio Schedule A (the Schedule of Adjustments); the 2021 form was not read.
2021.source_citation: R.C. 5747.01(A)(17), (A)(18) (current text, summarised by FindLaw; official codes.ohio.gov refused the connection); tax.ohio.gov FAQ 'Income - Bonus Depreciation' https://tax.ohio.gov/help-center/faqs/income-bonus-depreciation/income-bonus-depreciation (search excerpt only; fetch returned HTTP 404); 2025 IT 1040 instruction booklet pages 20, 22-23, 63 as the agency statement of the same rule; tax.ohio.gov/individual/file-now/ohio-conformity-updates (search excerpt)
2021.verify_note: Statute read only through a FindLaw summary (codes.ohio.gov ECONNREFUSED, Justia HTTP 403) and the agency FAQ only through a search excerpt (direct fetch 404). No 2021 Ohio form or booklet was read, so the rule is applied to 2021 from the current statute text and the 2025 booklet, not from a 2021 source. The 2012-or-later wording of the 2/3 rule does cover 2021.
2021.change_note: Ohio is a static-conformity state (R.C. 5701.11) updated by annual bills; tax.ohio.gov conformity table (via search excerpt): tax year 2021 prior effective date 31 Mar 2021, conformity date 17 Feb 2022, and the taxpayer may irrevocably elect either the IRC as of the close of the taxable year or the version to which Ohio conforms. The 168(k)/179 add-back sits outside the conformity election.
2021.special_rules: The 179 add-back is limited to 179 expense above 'the amount that would have been allowed under section 179 as it existed on Dec. 31, 2002' (2025 booklet p.20); the agency FAQ excerpt calls this $25,000. The 200,000 phase-out figure is the investment threshold of the 2002 federal text and is NOT stated by Ohio, so treat it as unconfirmed. Deduction of prior-year add-backs is taken in equal increments in consecutive years, any unused portion is not carried forward, it may be taken after disposing of the asset, and it is NOT allowed in a year with a federal NOL, NOL carryback or NOL carryforward (carried to the next year without one). No add-back for 168(k)/179 depreciation passed through from a pass-through entity (PTE) in which the taxpayer owns less than 5% (2025 booklet p.20, applied here as a continuing statute rule). These adjustments are not 'business income' (not on the Schedule of Business Income). Pass-through and fiduciary filers (IT 4708, IT 4738, IT 1041, IT 1140) make their own add-back and report it on the IT K-1. Nonresident and part-year filers apportion the depreciation adjustment by business through the IT NRC (property 20%, payroll 20%, sales 60%). Ohio has no state NOL carryback of its own but follows the federal carryback years, limited by the add-back. Commercial Activity Tax (CAT) is a gross receipts tax with no depreciation computation (not researched).
2021.override_note: batch6 note: Ohio adds back 5/6 of federal 168(k) and of Section 179 above the amount allowed under the Dec. 31, 2002 law ($25,000 / $200,000), then deducts 1/5 a year for five years (2025 IT 1040 booklet lines 9 and 27). The 2/3 variant (withholding increase) and 6/6 (NOL year) are not modelled. The $200,000 phase-out is the 2002 federal figure, not stated by Ohio.

2025.summary: 2025 IT 1040 instructions (read in full, tax year 2025, printed as accurate to 27 Nov 2025), Schedule of Adjustments line 9 'IRC 168(k) and 179 Depreciation' (p.20): 'Add 5/6 of your bonus depreciation allowed under Internal Revenue Code section 168(k). Also add 5/6 of your depreciation expense allowed under Internal Revenue Code section 179 less the amount that would have been allowed under section 179 as it existed on Dec. 31, 2002. Replace 5/6 with 2/3 for employers who increased their Ohio income taxes withheld by at least 10% over the previous year. Replace 5/6 with 6/6 for taxpayers who incur a net operating loss for federal income tax purposes if the loss was a result of the 168(k) and/or 179 depreciation expenses.' No add-back for an employer whose Ohio withholding rose by at least its total 168(k) and 179 expense, or for pass-through depreciation where the taxpayer owns less than 5%. 2021.summary: South Carolina does not adopt IRC 168(k): S.C. Code 12-6-50(4) lists 168(k), (l), (m) and (n) 'relating to bonus depreciation' among sections not adopted. 2021 SC1040 instructions, line v (p.18): 'South Carolina does not recognize bonus depreciation in IRC Section 168(k). With or without bonus depreciation, the depreciable life of the property is the same for federal and state purposes. For the tax year the property is placed in service, a taxpayer must add back, on line e of the SC1040, the difference between the depreciation deduction allowed for federal purposes and the deduction that would have been allowed without bonus depreciation. The South Carolina adjusted basis will then be greater than the federal adjusted basis. For all other years of the depreciable life of the property, an additional depreciation deduction is available for South Carolina purposes.' Line e (p.13) repeats the add-back. Net: SC depreciation = regular MACRS with no bonus.
